summary: Wendi L. Adamek is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies. She earned her PhD from Stanford University in 1998, studying under Michel Strickmann, Seizan Yanagida, and Hidehiko Koga. She held posts at Barnard College and the University of Calgary.

Wendy Doniger specializes in Indology, religious studies, and history/archaeology. She studied at Radcliffe, Harvard (PhD 1968 under Daniel H. H. Ingalls), and Oxford (D.Phil. 1973 under Robert Charles Zaehner). From 1978, she held a distinguished professorship at the University of Chicago.
Wenjiang Ding was a Chinese historian and archaeologist who studied under Qichao Liang and at Peking University. He later held an academic post at Peking University from around 1913 to 1917.

Wenjie Duan worked in Buddhist studies and history/archaeology after studying at Sichuan Fine Arts Institute and the Central Academy of Fine Arts. He held multiple leadership roles at Dunhuang Academy between 1946 and 1998, serving as its director in 1991.

Wenjie Qin is a scholar of Buddhist studies and religious studies who earned a PhD at Harvard University. Studies were completed under doctoral supervisor Wei-ming Tu as well as teachers Diana L. Eck, Masatoshi Nagatomi, Charles Hallisey, and Robert M. Gimello.

Werner Abraham was a linguist who studied at TU Wien, Innsbruck, and the University of Vienna, where he earned his PhD. He held posts at Illinois, Tübingen, and an ordinary professorship in German linguistics and medieval studies at Groningen from 1971.

Werner Sundermann was a scholar in Iranian and Central Asian studies as well as linguistics. Over his career, he held posts at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1967–1970), the Academy of Sciences of the GDR (~1970–1992), and Free University of Berlin (~1993–2000).
Wes Borton is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He studied at East Carolina University, working under teacher Derek F. Maher, and later studied at the University of Michigan.

Whalen Lai works in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies. After studying at International Christian University and Harvard University (PhD ~1968–1975), he held posts at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (~1976–1978) and UC Davis (~1978–2004).

Whitney Cox specializes in Indology and religious studies, having studied at the University of Virginia and the University of Chicago. Cox held academic posts at SOAS University of London (~2006–2014) and later as a professor at the University of Chicago from around 2014.

Wijesinghe Sugathadasa Karunaratne was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who completed his BA at the University of Ceylon and PhD at SOAS/University of London. He held posts at Ceylon (1952–1973) and the University of Kelaniya (~1956–1986).

Wilburn Hansen is a scholar of religious studies and Japanology. He completed a master's program at the University of Colorado Boulder and pursued further studies at Stanford University under teachers Bernard Faure and Carl Bielefeldt.

Wilfred Cantwell Smith was a religious studies scholar educated at Toronto, Cambridge, and Princeton (PhD ~1948). He held posts at Forman Christian College (1940–1946), McGill University from 1948, Dalhousie, and Harvard University (1964–1973, 1978–1985).

Wilfrid Sellars was a philosopher who studied at Buffalo, Michigan, and Oxford. He taught at the University of Iowa (1938–1946), University of Minnesota (1947–1958), and Yale University (1958–1963), before holding a professorship at the University of Pittsburgh (1963–1989).

Wilhelm Deecke was a linguist and Indologist who studied in Leipzig (Dr. phil. 1848–1849) and Berlin under scholars including Albrecht Weber and Franz Bopp. He later directed schools, including the Ernestinenschule (1855–1870) and Lycée Albert-Schweitzer Mulhouse (1889).

Wilhelm Dilthey was a philosopher who studied at Heidelberg University and Humboldt University of Berlin. He subsequently held academic posts at the universities of Basel (~1866–1868), Kiel (~1868–1871), Breslau (~1871–1882), and Berlin (~1882–1905).

Wilhelm Geiger was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Friedrich von Spiegel at Erlangen (PhD ~1876, Habilitation ~1878). He held professorships at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg from 1891 and the University of Munich (1920–1924).

Wilhelm Gesenius was a scholar of linguistics and religious studies. He studied at the University of Helmstedt (~1803–1806) and the University of Göttingen (~1806–1808), before holding posts at Göttingen (~1808–1810) and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1810–1842).

Wilhelm Grube was a scholar of Sinology and linguistics who studied at Saint Petersburg and Leipzig (PhD ~1880 under Georg von der Gabelentz). He worked at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin and became an extraordinary professor at Humboldt University of Berlin in 1892.
Wilhelm Gundert was a scholar in the fields of Japanology and religious studies who succeeded Karl Florenz. He held an academic post at the University of Hamburg from around 1936 to 1945.
